One-page synthesis

Core thesis: This case report documents an unusually severe, rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis caused by USA300 MRSA in a patient whose HIV/AIDS was first recognized during the hospitalization. The value of the report lies in the detailed clinical course, isolate susceptibility profile, molecular typing, histopathology, and comparison with prior reported MRSA necrotizing fasciitis cases.

The patient progressed from a recent axillary skin infection to septic shock and extensive necrotizing fasciitis requiring right-arm amputation, chest-wall debridement, transfer, and nine further debridements. MRSA was recovered from blood, sputum, wound, and subsequent surgical tissues. The isolate was resistant to clindamycin, erythromycin, levofloxacin, and methicillin; vancomycin MIC was 2 µg/mL. Molecular testing identified USA300/spa1 features, SCCmec IVa, ACME, and PVL genes, with alpha-hemolysin and PVL protein expression.

HIV testing was positive and the discharge CD4+ count was <20 cells/mm³ with HIV viral load 358,000 copies/mL. After the acute MRSA illness resolved, an HIV-related multidrug regimen was prescribed; one month later CD4+ count was 192 cells/mm³. The authors’ English-language literature review found 19 other reported MRSA necrotizing fasciitis cases, only one of which was HIV positive, and documented USA300 in five of those prior cases. These observations support recognition of USA300 MRSA as a possible necrotizing-fasciitis pathogen, but they do not establish HIV as a causal susceptibility factor or prove that PVL, ACME, clindamycin resistance, or a vancomycin MIC of 2 caused the extreme severity.

Scope warning: This is a single case plus secondary literature review, not a comparative treatment study. It is useful for phenotype recognition, microbiology, and hypothesis generation; it should not be used alone to infer treatment efficacy, HIV-specific risk magnitude, or causal virulence mechanisms.

Section-by-section condensation

Abstract

The abstract frames MRSA as a rarely reported cause of necrotizing fasciitis and presents this case as unusually severe in a patient with previously undiagnosed AIDS. It also foregrounds the molecular finding that the isolate had the USA300/spa1 genotype.

Case presentation and acute management

The patient presented with severe right-arm symptoms and shock after two weeks of unresolved axillary hidradenitis treated with clindamycin. Initial BP was 58/32 mm Hg, pulse 130/min, temperature 99.4°F, and WBC 1,600/µL. Empiric vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and clindamycin did not prevent rapid deterioration requiring ventilation, fluids, vasopressors, and surgery within 24 hours.

Extensive necrosis led to right-arm amputation and chest-wall debridement. Cultures grew MRSA; therapy was changed to vancomycin, imipenem/cilastatin, rifampin, and voriconazole. Disease nevertheless spread across the chest walls, right abdomen, and back. The patient underwent nine additional debridements after transfer and ultimately improved enough for rehabilitation.

HIV/AIDS findings

HIV infection was newly identified during the diagnostic workup. At discharge, CD4+ count was <20 cells/mm³ and viral load 358,000 copies/mL. The authors describe initiation of tenofovir, lamivudine, atazanavir, ritonavir, dapsone, and azithromycin after resolution of the MRSA infection; one month later CD4+ count was 192 cells/mm³.

Molecular characterization

The blood isolate was characterized by spa sequencing, multiplex PCR, and Western immunoblotting. Results were consistent with USA300 and spa type 1; PCR detected SCCmec IVa, ACME, and lukS-lukF encoding PVL. Immunoblotting confirmed alpha-hemolysin and PVL expression.

The authors place these findings in the context of contemporary USA300 epidemiology and possible virulence. Importantly, they acknowledge that epidemiologic and experimental evidence had not unambiguously demonstrated a direct role for PVL or ACME in invasive disease.

Literature comparison and discussion

The authors identified 19 other English-language reports of MRSA necrotizing fasciitis; one of those 19 patients was HIV positive. Their comparison table includes the index patient plus the 19 prior cases and reports USA300 in the index case and five others.

The discussion argues for including USA300 MRSA in the differential diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis and warns that apparently benign MRSA skin infections may progress rapidly. It also speculates that constitutive clindamycin resistance and an increased vancomycin MIC could have contributed to treatment failure, while explicitly describing the therapeutic significance as uncertain.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Skim deeply. High value as a memorable clinical/microbiologic case and historical USA300 signal; low evidentiary weight for treatment or causal risk inference.
Relevance: 8/10

Directly relevant to severe MRSA infection, source control, susceptibility interpretation, and HIV-associated infectious disease.

Basis: Detailed case course, cultures, MIC table, genotype, histology.
Main limit: Single historical case.
Would change: Would rise with a modern multi-center case series or guideline linkage.
Novelty: 7/10

At publication, the combination of USA300 MRSA necrotizing fasciitis and previously unrecognized AIDS was unusual.

Basis: Molecular characterization and comparison with prior cases.
Main limit: Case novelty decays as epidemiology changes.
Would change: Would rise if a unique mechanism or prospectively validated phenotype were demonstrated.
Method strength: 3/10

Clinical and laboratory description is detailed, but the design is an uncontrolled case report with a narrative literature review.

Basis: Culture, MIC, molecular typing, histology.
Main limit: No comparator, prespecified protocol, or inferential statistics.
Would change: Would rise with systematic case ascertainment and comparative design.
Evidence strength: 3/10

Strong evidence that this patient had the described infection and isolate phenotype; weak evidence for causal virulence or treatment claims.

Basis: Concordant clinical, microbiologic, pathologic, and genotypic observations.
Main limit: n=1 and causal confounding.
Would change: Would rise with replicated comparative cohorts and mechanistic validation.
External validity: 2/10

The index case is extreme and cannot define expected risk or outcomes for broader MRSA or HIV populations.

Basis: One adult case plus heterogeneous published reports.
Main limit: Selection/publication bias and incomplete historical testing.
Would change: Would rise with population-based surveillance using standardized definitions.
Implementation value: 5/10

Useful for recognition and diagnostic vigilance, but not sufficient to set antimicrobial or HIV-specific management policy.

Basis: Highlights rapid progression, need for source control, and susceptibility/genotype context.
Main limit: Historical treatment era and no treatment comparison.
Would change: Would rise with integration into current guideline evidence and contemporary susceptibility data.

Validity and bias

Internal validity for descriptive facts: moderate-to-high for the individual patient because cultures, pathology, MIC testing, and molecular assays converge. Causal validity: low. The report cannot establish whether AIDS, USA300 genotype, PVL, ACME, clindamycin resistance, vancomycin MIC, timing of surgery, or another factor caused the extraordinary severity. Treatment changes occurred alongside repeated surgery and critical care, preventing attribution of improvement to any one drug or regimen.

Publication and selection bias: extreme cases are preferentially reported. The 19-case comparison is based on published English-language cases, with many unknown fields and no reproducible systematic-review method stated, so prevalence-like inferences should be avoided.

Implementation / practice takeaways

Use now

Retain as a recognition case: invasive MRSA can present with fulminant necrotizing fasciitis and septic shock, and aggressive source control may be required.

Do not overclaim

Do not infer that HIV/AIDS independently predisposes to MRSA necrotizing fasciitis from this report, or that PVL/ACME caused the severity.

Antimicrobial interpretation

Table 1 documents the isolate phenotype, including clindamycin resistance and vancomycin MIC 2 µg/mL. It does not test comparative regimen efficacy.

Read next

Prioritize the cited MRSA-necrotizing-fasciitis case literature and more recent guidelines/cohorts before translating this historical case into current practice.

Clinical action boundary: This SEA artifact summarizes and appraises the 2008 source. Current treatment decisions require contemporary guidance, patient-specific microbiology, source-control assessment, and local susceptibility data.
